summary: Specifies how to use the HSS/LMS hash-based signature algorithm, described in RFC 8554, with CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE). Hash-based signatures are one family of digital signatures.

eli5.summary: A way of signing messages using a stack of one-time stamps, written down in the way small devices like to use.

questions: how to use lms signatures with cose
how to use hash-based signatures with cose
what is the cose algorithm value for hss-lms
why are hash-based signatures post-quantum secure
subtitle: How to sign COSE messages with HSS/LMS hash-based signatures, which are designed to survive quantum computers.

tldr.problem: Widely used signature algorithms such as RSA, DSA, ECDSA and EdDSA would be vulnerable if large-scale quantum computers are ever built, so a post-quantum option is needed.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines how the HSS/LMS hash-based signature algorithm from RFC 8554 is carried in COSE: a new algorithm entry, a new key type and a public key parameter, with the signature as a single large byte string.
tldr.outcome: COSE can now carry HSS/LMS signatures, for example to protect software updates. Signers must track which one-time keys they have used, because reuse breaks security.

today: RFC 8778 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 8554 and RFC 8152.

sections.title: Why Hash-Based Signatures in COSE
sections.content:
This RFC specifies how to use the Hierarchical Signature System (HSS) / Leighton-Micali Signature (LMS) algorithm with CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE). The algorithm itself is defined in RFC 8554; this document only says how it fits into COSE.

The text lists the trade-offs. The algorithm can only be used for a fixed number of signing operations, which depends on the size of the tree. Public keys are small and the computational cost is low, but the signatures are quite large. The private key can be very small if the signer accepts extra computation at signing time, or larger and faster. HSS/LMS signatures are currently defined to use exclusively SHA-256.
sections.eli5: It is a new kind of signature that works with hash functions, and it comes with a rule: you only get a certain number of signatures, and each one is big.

sections.title: The Post-Quantum Motivation
sections.content:
Advances in cryptanalysis and progress on quantum computers threaten widely deployed signature algorithms. If large-scale quantum computers are ever built, they will be able to break many public-key cryptosystems in use. The RFC names RSA, DSA, ECDSA and EdDSA as all being vulnerable in that case, and says when such computers will be feasible is open to conjecture.

HSS/LMS does not depend on the difficulty of discrete logarithms or factoring, so it is considered post-quantum secure. The RFC suggests using it to protect software update distribution. That would let future software that implements new cryptosystems be authenticated and integrity protected, even if advances break today's signature mechanisms.
sections.eli5: Some day, very powerful computers might be able to forge today's signatures. This kind of signature is built from a different idea, so those computers should not fool it.

sections.title: How HSS/LMS Is Built
sections.content:
The algorithm has three layers. LM-OTS is a one-time signature method. LMS puts many one-time keys in a tree, with 2^h leaves for a tree of height h. HSS arranges a hierarchy of such trees, so lower trees can be generated when needed instead of building one huge tree, which might take weeks or longer.

An HSS signature carries the number of signed public keys (Nspk), then that many signed public keys, then the LMS signature over the message. The top tree's public key is the public key of the whole HSS system. A parent tree's key signs the child tree's public key, and the bottom tree's key signs the message.

An LMS signature has four elements: the leaf number, an LM-OTS signature, a type code and an array of sibling values along the path to the root. RFC 8554 supports tree heights h=5, 10, 15, 20 and 25, and the hash output size is m=32 bytes with SHA-256. LM-OTS supports Winternitz widths w=1, 2, 4 and 8.
sections.eli5: Think of a family tree of stamp books. The top book vouches for the books below it, and the bottom book signs your letter. You make new books only when you need them.

sections.title: Algorithm Identifiers and COSE Keys
sections.content:
COSE supports two signature schemes, and this document uses the signature with appendix scheme. The signature value is one large byte string. It is designed for easy parsing, because counters and type codes inside it indirectly give all the information needed to parse it during validation.

When a COSE key is used for this algorithm, the receiver checks several fields:

  • kty MUST be HSS-LMS.
  • If alg is present, it MUST be HSS-LMS.
  • If key_ops is present, it MUST include sign when creating a signature and verify when verifying one.
  • If kid is present, it MAY identify the top of the HSS tree. In RFC 8554 this identifier is called I, the 16-byte identifier of the LMS public key for the tree.
sections.eli5: The label on the key must say it is an HSS-LMS key, and it must be allowed to sign if you are signing, or to check if you are checking.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations MUST protect the private keys, because compromise can allow forged signatures. They MUST also keep track of which leaf nodes have been used. If that tracking data loses integrity, a one-time key can be used more than once. Failed writes, virtual machine snapshotting or cloning and similar operational problems must be considered when keys and tracking data sit on nonvolatile media or in a virtual machine.

Each LMS key pair in the HSS tree MUST be generated independently of all others. An LM-OTS private key MUST be used to generate a signature only once and MUST NOT be used for anything else.

Private key generation relies on random numbers. Poor pseudorandom number generators can leave little or no security, because an attacker may search a small set of possibilities. Signature generation also uses random numbers, with much less severe consequences from a weak generator. The RFC points to RFC 4086 for guidance.
sections.eli5: Never use the same one-time stamp twice, and keep careful notes about which ones you used. Also, pick your secret stamps with truly random dice.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
The HSS root public key is the public key for the signature. Without a public key infrastructure it acts as a trust anchor. The number of signatures is bounded by the size of the HSS set of trees, and once all LM-OTS signatures are used, a new trust anchor must be established.

The signer keeps state across signing operations so that no tree node signs twice. RFC 8554 describes practical approaches, and in some of them nodes are sacrificed, so the usable number of signatures may be smaller than the full tree allows.

This RFC deliberately defines no COSE Key Type Parameter for the private key and its usage state. That avoids making it easy to save the key and state, sign, and then restore the old state, which the text calls disastrous because it enables tree node reuse.
sections.eli5: When all the stamps are used up, you need a whole new stamp book and everyone must be told to trust it. That is why nobody is allowed to photocopy the book and its notes to go back in time.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA added three entries. In the COSE Algorithms registry: name HSS-LMS, value -46, marked Recommended. In the COSE Key Types registry: name HSS-LMS, value 5, for the public key. In the COSE Key Type Parameters registry: key type 5, name pub, label -1, CBOR type bstr.

Appendix A gives two non-normative examples in CBOR diagnostic notation, a full message signature of 2560 bytes and a COSE_Sign1 message of 2552 bytes, both with the payload 'This is the content.'. Their size shows how large these signatures are.
sections.eli5: The official list of names and numbers now has entries for this signature type, so everyone uses the same labels.
